title: the seasons
hook: frost on the windshield and a bigger appetite: Charaka's chapter on the seasons has a reason for both

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seasons: a year in two halves, adana, the taking, and visarga, the giving.

Frost on a car windshield before work. Breath you can see. And by lunch, a hunger bigger than it was in summer, as if the body quietly raised its order. A bowl of something hot tastes better than it has any right to. That's usually filed under comfort food and left there. But the Charaka Samhita, one of Ayurveda's classical texts, gives the cold months a careful reading, and the bigger appetite sits right at its center. After oil, movement and good conduct, this week has walked out to the year itself. Today, the cold.
screen: `FROST ON THE WINDSHIELD.` → `A BIGGER APPETITE.` → `TODAY, THE COLD.`

segments.voice: Charaka's chapter on the seasons names two winters: hemanta, early winter, and shishira, late winter, colder and harsher. Its observation, paraphrased: in the cold, the body's fire of digestion is held in by the cold outside, and it grows strong, strong enough for heavy, substantial food. Then a sharper line. If that strong fire isn't given proper food, the text says, it turns on the body's own tissues. So winter isn't the season for skimping. The advice is warm and generous: substantial food with some richness, warm water, oil rubbed into the skin, heavy clothes, warm rooms, the sun when it's out. Three things follow. First, it's the rule from the dosha days: like increases like, and the opposite brings it down. Cold is met with warmth, dry winter air with oil. Second, the appetite isn't a fault to fight. It's the body doing its job in the cold, and the job is to feed it well. Third, the festivals sit close by. In parts of India, at Makar Sankranti in midwinter, people share sweets of sesame and jaggery, and in Maharashtra they say, roughly, take this sweet and speak sweetly. Winter food at a winter festival, given away. None of this asks you to live in an Indian winter. It asks you to look at the season you're actually in, and answer it.
screen: `HEMANTA AND SHISHIRA, THE COLD MONTHS` · `A STRONG FIRE IN THE COLD` · `FEED IT, OR IT FEEDS ON YOU` · `SESAME AND JAGGERY AT SANKRANTI`

segments.voice: Find the warmest place in the body right now, the folded hands, the chest or the belly, and rest your attention there, feeling the out-breath warm as it leaves. If there's cold at the edges, at the feet or the back of the neck, notice it without fixing it: warmth in the middle, weather at the edges. If you pray, give thanks for the last warm meal you ate.
The seasons. In winter, Charaka's reading is a strong inner fire held in by the cold, one that needs real food. Today's word.
Your line: the seasons. Winter's strong fire asks to be fed, and fed well. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: People who follow Ayurveda adjust food and habits through the year as the classical texts describe; in the cold months that means substantial warm food, oil on the skin and warm clothing, and in parts of India families share sesame-and-jaggery sweets at Makar Sankranti.
